jobs.pdf_summary_text: A total of {total} potential schedule conflicts were identified on server {server}: {critical} critical, {warning} warnings. Over the analysis period, {collisions} job pairs actually collided, with {failures} of those collisions resulting in failures. This document details each conflict, its root cause, impact, and recommended improvement.
jobs.pdf_cause_same_type: Two or more jobs of the same type (DBCC, Backup, Index Rebuild, etc.) are scheduled at the same time. When they execute simultaneously, they compete for the same I/O, CPU, and system lock resources.
jobs.pdf_impact_same_type: Same-type jobs running in parallel cause severe resource contention: increased disk latency, prolonged locks, timeouts, and potential failure of one or both jobs. On large databases, this can cause visible degradation for end users.
jobs.pdf_improvement_same_type: By separating schedules or chaining jobs sequentially (using sp_add_jobstep), each job runs with exclusive access to needed resources. This reduces I/O contention by up to 50%, eliminates deadlocks between same-type jobs, and ensures each job completes faster with lower failure probability.
jobs.pdf_cause_concurrent_backups: Multiple backups (Full, Differential, Log) are scheduled at overlapping times. Concurrent backups generate massive sequential I/O load on disk, as each needs to read the entire database or transaction log.
jobs.pdf_impact_concurrent_backups: Concurrent backups can double or triple I/O load on the server. This results in: 2-3x longer backup times, performance degradation for production queries, possible backup failure due to timeout, and risk of insufficient backup window.
jobs.pdf_improvement_concurrent_backups: Staggering backups sequentially (Full first, then Differential, then Log) ensures each operation has optimal disk access. This reduces total backup time, minimizes production impact window, and eliminates failures caused by I/O contention between backups.
jobs.pdf_cause_concurrent_maintenance: Maintenance jobs (Index Rebuild, Statistics Update, DBCC CheckDB, Shrink) are running at the same time. These operations are I/O and CPU intensive, and when concurrent, they amplify each other's impact.
jobs.pdf_impact_concurrent_maintenance: Concurrent maintenance causes extreme CPU and I/O usage spikes, potentially saturating the server. Index Rebuild with simultaneous DBCC CheckDB can lock entire tables, cause lock escalation, and make the database temporarily unavailable for normal operations.
jobs.pdf_improvement_concurrent_maintenance: Distributing maintenance operations across different time slots (preferably overnight, sequentially) allows each operation to complete without interference. This results in more efficient maintenance, lower server impact, and better availability windows for users.
jobs.pdf_cause_different_types: Jobs of different types are scheduled at the same time. Although they don't directly compete for the same resources, the combined load may exceed server capacity during that period.
jobs.pdf_impact_different_types: Simultaneous execution of different job types (e.g., Backup + Index Rebuild) can cause temporary load spikes. The impact is generally less than same-type conflicts, but on resource-limited servers it can cause noticeable slowdowns.
jobs.pdf_improvement_different_types: Redistributing schedules to avoid overlap reduces load spikes and distributes work more evenly throughout the day. On resource-limited servers, this simple change can significantly improve stability.
jobs.pdf_help_critical: Same-type jobs or concurrent backups competing for the same resources — high failure risk.
jobs.pdf_help_warning: Concurrent maintenance jobs that may cause load spikes — medium risk.
jobs.pdf_help_collisions: Job pairs that actually collided (ran at the same time) in recent days, confirmed by execution history.
jobs.pdf_help_failures: Real collisions that resulted in failure of at least one job — direct operational impact.
jobs.pdf_help_collision_table: This table shows job pairs that actually ran simultaneously. 'Collisions' indicates how many times it happened, 'Avg Overlap' the average simultaneous execution time, and 'Failures' how many of those collisions caused an error.
jobs.pdf_help_action_plan: Each recommendation includes: root cause, system impact, recommended action, why it will improve, and ready-to-execute SQL commands. Recommendations are sorted by severity (critical > warning > info).
jobs.pdf_section1_intro: The following problems were identified in the SQL Server Agent Jobs of instance {server} through schedule analysis, execution history and real collision detection between jobs.
jobs.pdf_section2_intro: The following table shows job pairs that actually ran simultaneously in the last {days} days, confirmed by SQL Server Agent execution history.
jobs.pdf_section3_intro: For each identified conflict, the following details the cause, impact, recommended action, technical justification, and ready-to-execute SQL commands.

jobs.pdf_risk_job_longer: Job takes longer than expected after change
jobs.pdf_risk_job_longer_mitigation: Monitor durations; adjust gaps between jobs if needed
jobs.pdf_risk_new_conflict: New collision between jobs after rescheduling
jobs.pdf_rollback_intro: All changes are reversible. Simply re-execute the SQL commands with original values or re-enable disabled jobs.
jobs.pdf_checklist_rerun_analysis: Re-run conflict analysis to validate resolution

kpi_modal.verdict_help:
What it is: each database gets an integrity verdict.
P1 Corrupted: damaged pages detected - act now.
P3 Never validated: CHECKDB has never run.
P4 Stale validation: last CHECKDB over 30 days ago.
P5 OK: recently validated.
Why it matters: corruption is silent - it only shows up when it already hurts. CHECKDB is the routine exam that catches it early.
What to do: click a verdict to filter the list; each card includes a ready-to-run command. If collection failed, the card shows the exact error.

mem.help_100_desc: Seeing 100% on this card is expected and healthy! It means SQL Server is using all the memory configured for it. SQL Server is designed to consume and keep memory in cache for better performance.
mem.help_available_desc: Available: Memory that can be immediately allocated. When it's 0 GB, Windows is using it all as File Cache (Standby) - this is normal and reclaimable.
mem.help_buffer_pool: Buffer Pool: Memory currently used by SQL Server for data and index cache.
mem.help_critical_desc: CRITICAL vs Normal: CRITICAL status appears when available memory is < 5% of total RAM. If OS/Cache is high, it may not be a real problem.
mem.help_max_not_configured: If Max Server Memory is not configured (using default 2TB)
mem.help_max_server: Max Server Memory: Maximum configured limit. SQL Server will not use more than this value.
mem.help_memory_pressure: If there is Memory Pressure (SQL needing more memory than available)
mem.help_oom_desc: OOM (Out-of-Memory): Corresponds to Event ID 701. Indicates queries failed due to lack of memory in the pool.
mem.help_os_desc: OS Memory shows the server's total physical memory and how it is distributed between SQL Server, other processes, and Windows.
mem.help_oscache_desc: OS/Cache (Standby): Windows uses free memory as disk cache. It is reclaimable when needed. Not a problem.
mem.help_pageiolatch: If PAGEIOLATCH waits are high (indicates insufficient memory for cache)
mem.help_rg_desc: Resource Governor is a SQL Server feature that allows limiting and managing CPU and memory allocation between different workloads.
mem.pressure_critical_desc: SQL Server is using significantly less memory than allocated. This may indicate serious issues:
mem.pressure_critical_increase: Consider increasing Max Server Memory if RAM is available
mem.pressure_healthy_buffer: The Buffer Pool is well utilized
mem.pressure_healthy_monitor: Continue monitoring to ensure the value stays above 95%.
mem.pressure_na_action_check: Check if SQL Server is online and running
mem.pressure_na_action_queries: Run some queries on the server to force memory allocation
mem.pressure_na_desc: SQL Server has not yet allocated enough memory to calculate Memory Pressure. This can happen in some scenarios:
mem.pressure_na_fresh: Recently started instance: SQL Server is in "warm-up" process and has not yet loaded data into the Buffer Pool
mem.pressure_na_low_activity: Low activity: No active queries forcing SQL Server to allocate memory
mem.pressure_na_pending: Data collection pending: Data may not yet have been collected by the monitoring system
mem.pressure_na_target_zero: Target Server Memory = 0: The performance counter "Target Server Memory (KB)" has not been calculated yet
mem.pressure_warning_desc: SQL Server is using less memory than it could. This may indicate:
mem.pressure_warning_maxmem: Consider reviewing Max Server Memory configuration
mem.pressure_warning_slow: Check for slow queries that could benefit from more cache
mem.pressure_warning_warmup: SQL Server has not fully "warmed up" yet
